title: The western princes cross the Volga
place: Middle and lower Volga and the western steppe

sides.opponent: Volga Bulgars, Kipchaks (Cumans) and neighbouring peoples

summary: Ögedei sent the senior grandsons of Chinggis Khan west under Batu, with Subutai as field commander. In 1236 their combined army crossed the Volga and turned on the Volga Bulgars and the Kipchak steppe.
detail: The Secret History records that Ögedei sent the eldest sons of each princely line to reinforce Subutai. Batu, Büri, Güyük and Möngke were among them. Their task was to cross the Volga and the Ural rivers and subdue the peoples beyond, from the Kipchaks to the Rus' and the Hungarians. The army that gathered in 1236 drew troops from every branch of the family. Its first targets were the Volga Bulgars, whose trading towns controlled the fur route up the river, and the Kipchak clans of the steppe. Rus' chronicles and Rashid al-Din describe the Bulgar towns being taken and burned in the autumn, and Möngke went on to hunt down the Kipchak leader Bachman on the lower Volga. Refugees from both peoples fled west ahead of the armies.
significance: This campaign began the Great Western Campaign, which within six years reached Poland, Hungary and the Adriatic and created the Jochid khanate (the Golden Horde).
uncertaintyNote: The westward campaign and the Volga crossing are secure. The pack deliberately leaves out the destruction of Bolghar, Bilär and Saqsin because that needs a second primary witness. The Laurentian Chronicle and Rashid al-Din report it, but details, dates (autumn 1236 or 1237) and which 'Great City' fell are disputed. Army size is unknown: modern estimates run from about 30,000–50,000 Mongol troops to older figures of 120,000 or more.
sources: Secret History of the Mongols §§270,274 (de Rachewiltz translation pp.190-194)
Rashid al-Din, Jami' al-Tawarikh
Laurentian Chronicle
Juvaini, History of the World-Conqueror
Allsen, Mongol Imperialism
May, The Mongol Conquests in World History

title: Siege and capture of Ryazan
summary: Ryazan was the first Rus' city the invasion reached. The Mongols surrounded it, broke in, and took it in December 1237.
detail: The Mongols came out of the steppe in early winter, when frozen rivers could carry an army. Their envoys demanded a tenth of everything the principality had. Ryazan refused and asked Vladimir for help, which never arrived. The Novgorod First Chronicle describes the Mongols encircling the city with a palisade and fighting their way in. Prince Yuri Igorevich died, and the city was destroyed. Old Ryazan was never rebuilt as a capital; the princely seat later moved to Pereyaslavl-Ryazansky, today's Ryazan. Archaeologists have excavated burnt houses and mass burials at the old site, Staraya Ryazan, on the high bank of the Oka.
significance: Ryazan set the pattern for the invasion of Rus': an ultimatum, a winter siege, and destruction where there was resistance.
uncertaintyNote: Chronicle tradition dates the siege to 16–21 December 1237. The pack keeps the event to month precision and leaves out the day and the accounts of total massacre. The later 'Tale of the Destruction of Ryazan', with its hero Evpaty Kolovrat, is a literary work of much later date.
sources: Novgorod First Chronicle, Synodal Text, A.M. 6746 (Michell & Forbes trans., 1914, pp.81-82)
Laurentian Chronicle
Fennell, The Crisis of Medieval Russia 1200–1304
Martin, Medieval Russia 980–1584

title: Battle of the Sit River
place: Sit River corridor, north of the upper Volga
summary: A Mongol force caught Grand Prince Yuri II's army in its camp on the Sit River and destroyed it. Yuri was killed.
detail: Yuri had left his capital to gather an army on the Sit, a forest river that flows into the Mologa, and was waiting for his brothers' contingents to arrive. Meanwhile Vladimir itself was stormed in February 1238 and his family died in the burning cathedral. Then Mongol troops, led by Burundai according to later tradition, found his camp before he was ready. The chronicles say Yuri was killed in the fighting. His nephew Vasilko of Rostov was taken prisoner, refused to join his captors, and was put to death. With the grand prince dead, the surviving princes of north-eastern Rus', led by Yuri's brother Yaroslav, had no choice but to make terms with Batu.
significance: Yuri II's death ended organised resistance in north-eastern Rus' and made submission to the khan the only route to power there.
uncertaintyNote: The chronicles give 4 March 1238. The pack treats the location as a river corridor, not a point: several sites on the Sit have been proposed and the fighting may have involved more than one camp. The shaded area is indicative only. Force sizes are unknown. The fall of Vladimir (3–7 February 1238), which has no separate pack row, is mentioned here as context.
sources: Novgorod First Chronicle, Synodal Text, A.M. 6746 (Michell & Forbes trans., 1914, p.83)
Laurentian Chronicle
Fennell, The Crisis of Medieval Russia 1200–1304

title: Siege and capture of Kozelsk
summary: On its way back south in spring 1238, Batu's army was held up at the small town of Kozelsk, whose defenders chose to resist. The town was eventually taken.
detail: After turning back from the road to Novgorod, the Mongol army swung south towards the steppe. It reached Kozelsk, a small fortified town of the Chernigov lands. Its prince, Vasily, was still a child, and the townspeople decided to fight. The Galician–Volhynian Chronicle praises their stubborn defence, which included sorties against the besiegers' engines, and says the town fell only when reinforcements joined the attack. Rashid al-Din also records a long siege there. Kozelsk became the great symbol of Rus' resistance to the invasion. Tradition says the Mongols afterwards called it the 'Evil City'.
significance: Kozelsk was a rare check on the Mongol advance, and it became the most celebrated story of Rus' resistance.
uncertaintyNote: The pack confirms the siege and capture but leaves out the chronicle's duration (seven weeks), its figure of 4,000 Mongol dead, and its account of the whole population being killed. The seven weeks are usually placed between late March and May 1238. The 'Evil City' name comes through Rashid al-Din's 'Mo-Balïq' and later tradition.
sources: Galician-Volhynian Chronicle, second part, Batu/Kozelsk episode (Teofil Kostruba trans., 1936, pp.14-16 web text)
Rashid al-Din, Jami' al-Tawarikh
Fennell, The Crisis of Medieval Russia 1200–1304

title: Capture of Pereiaslav
summary: In March 1239 the Mongols opened their campaign against southern Rus' by taking Pereiaslav, the frontier city facing the steppe.
detail: After a year on the steppe fighting the Kipchaks and resting their horses, the Mongol princes turned on the southern Rus' principalities. Pereiaslav, south-east of Kiev, had guarded the Rus' frontier against the steppe nomads for two centuries. It was taken in early March 1239. The chronicles record the church of St Michael plundered and Bishop Simeon killed. The city lost its importance and never regained its former standing. With Pereiaslav gone, the left bank of the Dnieper lay open.
significance: Pereiaslav's fall began the southern Rus' campaign that led to Chernihiv and Kiev.
uncertaintyNote: 3 March 1239 is the date in the Rus' chronicle tradition. The commanders are not named in the Rus' sources. Rashid al-Din credits different princes with different operations in 1238–39, and the attribution is uncertain.
sources: Galician-Volhynian Chronicle, second part, Pereiaslav/Chernihiv episodes (Teofil Kostruba trans., 1936, pp.14-16 web text)
Laurentian Chronicle
Fennell, The Crisis of Medieval Russia 1200–1304
Martin, Medieval Russia 980–1584

title: Siege and capture of Chernihiv
summary: In autumn 1239 the Mongols besieged Chernihiv, seat of one of the great Rus' princely houses. A relief army under Prince Mstislav Glebovich was defeated and the city fell.
detail: Chernihiv on the Desna was one of the oldest and richest cities of Rus'. When the Mongols surrounded it, Prince Mstislav Glebovich came to its relief and was beaten outside the walls. The Galician–Volhynian Chronicle describes a hard siege: the defenders dropped huge stones from the ramparts, and the Mongols answered with stone-throwers of remarkable range. The city fell and was burned. Bishop Porfiry was taken captive and later released. The collapse of Chernihiv, following that of Pereiaslav, left Kiev isolated on the Dnieper.
significance: The fall of Chernihiv broke the second great southern principality and prepared the attack on Kiev in 1240.
uncertaintyNote: 18 October 1239 is the chronicle date. Some reconstructions place the defeat of the relief force before the siege, others during it. Which Mongol princes commanded is uncertain.
sources: Galician-Volhynian Chronicle, second part, Pereiaslav/Chernihiv episodes (Teofil Kostruba trans., 1936, pp.14-16 web text)
Laurentian Chronicle
Rashid al-Din, Jami' al-Tawarikh
Fennell, The Crisis of Medieval Russia 1200–1304

title: Capture of Kiev
summary: At the end of 1240 the combined western army besieged and took Kiev, the old mother city of Rus'. The Secret History lists it among the cities the princes conquered.
detail: Kiev had lost much of its political weight by 1240, but it was still the religious heart of Rus' and a great city. It was held for Daniel of Galicia by his commander Dmitr. The Mongols brought their whole army and their siege engines against it. The Galician–Volhynian Chronicle says the noise of their carts and herds drowned out speech in the city. The walls were broken, the defenders fought on behind an inner line, and the last of them died when the crowded Church of the Tithes collapsed. Batu is said to have spared the wounded Dmitr for his courage. In 1246 the papal envoy Carpini passed through and found a shrunken town surrounded by the bones of the dead.
significance: The fall of Kiev ended the city's standing as the centre of Rus' and opened the way to Galicia, Poland and Hungary.
uncertaintyNote: The pack's witness (Secret History §274) confirms that Kiev was taken but not the day. The Galician–Volhynian Chronicle's St Nicholas's Day (6 December 1240) is traditional; another reckoning gives 19 November. The pack leaves out details of the sack pending a Rus' witness; the narrative above follows the Galician–Volhynian Chronicle and Carpini. Some archaeologists think Kiev recovered faster than Carpini implies.
sources: Secret History of the Mongols §274 (de Rachewiltz translation pp.194-195)
Hypatian (Galician–Volhynian) Chronicle
John of Plano Carpini, Ystoria Mongalorum
Rashid al-Din, Jami' al-Tawarikh
Fennell, The Crisis of Medieval Russia 1200–1304

title: Battle of Legnica (Liegnitz)

sides.opponent: Duchy of Silesia and allied Polish forces

summary: A Mongol detachment that had crossed Lesser Poland met Duke Henry II of Silesia near Legnica. His army was defeated and he was killed.
detail: While Batu's main army invaded Hungary, a smaller Mongol force swept through Poland to stop the Polish princes from helping King Béla IV. In February and March it burned Sandomierz and Kraków and destroyed the knights of Lesser Poland at Chmielnik. Then it entered Silesia. Duke Henry II the Pious, the most powerful Polish prince, gathered what forces he could and gave battle near Legnica. The Greater Poland Chronicle records the Mongol victory and Henry's death in the fighting. Długosz's much later annal gives the fuller, dramatic narrative that most retellings follow. After the battle the Mongols turned south through Moravia to rejoin the army in Hungary.
significance: Legnica eliminated Polish and Silesian resistance so that no northern help reached Hungary. It became one of medieval Europe's emblematic disasters.
uncertaintyNote: 9 April 1241 is the accepted date. The pack keeps to the battle and its outcome and leaves out troop numbers, the make-up of Henry's army (the part played by the military orders is disputed), tactics such as Długosz's smokescreen, miraculous episodes, and casualty totals. Much of the popular story comes from Długosz two centuries later. Rashid al-Din names Baidar and Orda as commanders; some accounts add Qadan. The marker is at Legnickie Pole, the traditional battlefield. Some scholars prefer another site near the city.

title: Battle of Mohi (the Sajó River)
place: Sajó crossing and Hungarian camp near Mohi
summary: While the Hungarians guarded the Sajó bridge, the Mongols crossed the river elsewhere, surrounded King Béla IV's fortified camp, and destroyed the royal army as it broke and fled.
detail: Béla IV had led his army north-east from Pest to meet the Mongols and camped on the heath at Mohi, behind a tight ring of wagons, with the Sajó River in front. Master Roger, a canon who lived through the invasion, tells how the Mongols forced their way across the river away from the guarded bridge and came at the camp from several sides. The king's brother Koloman and Archbishop Ugrin fought hard, but most of the army stayed in the laager until it was surrounded. When the Hungarians broke out, they were cut down along the road to Pest. Béla escaped to Austria. Koloman later died of his wounds, and two archbishops were among the dead.
significance: Mohi destroyed Hungary's royal army and left the kingdom open to a year of Mongol occupation. It was the decisive battle of the invasion of Europe.
uncertaintyNote: The date (11 April, two days after Legnica) is secure. The pack leaves out casualty totals, which are unreliable, as are the numbers on both sides. Roger, Thomas of Split and Rashid al-Din differ on who crossed where. The Yuanshi biography of Subutai records a quarrel between Batu and Subutai over the delay at the bridge. The shaded area covers the crossing and camp region; there is no exact battle point.
sources: Master Roger, Carmen Miserabile chs. 28-30 (Latin text, Bibliotheca Augustana; event sequence also in CEU Press 2010 trans.)
Thomas of Split, Historia Salonitana
Rashid al-Din, Jami' al-Tawarikh
Yuanshi (biography of Subutai)
Jackson, The Mongols and the West
Sverdrup, The Mongol Conquests

title: Across the frozen Danube, the pursuit to Dalmatia, and the withdrawal
place: Western Hungary, Dalmatia, the western Balkans and Bulgaria

sides.opponent: Kingdom of Hungary–Croatia, the Dalmatian towns, Serbia and Bulgaria

summary: When the Danube froze in the winter of 1241, the Mongols crossed into western Hungary. Qadan chased Béla IV to the Dalmatian coast, and in spring 1242 the armies withdrew through the western Balkans and Bulgaria.
detail: For months the Danube had shielded western Hungary. Around Christmas 1241 it froze, and the Mongols crossed. They sacked Esztergom, although its citadel held, and ravaged the country around. Qadan took a force south through Croatia after the fugitive king. Thomas of Split watched the Mongols try to scale the crag of Klis, and ride along the shore at Trogir, where Béla had taken refuge on the islands out of reach. Then the order came to withdraw. Qadan's men went south along the coast, burning Kotor and attacking towns in Zeta. They then crossed Serbia, and the armies left through Bulgaria, which accepted Mongol overlordship, back to the Pontic steppe.
significance: The withdrawal ended the Great Western Campaign and left the Mongol frontier on the lower Danube. Béla's escape allowed the Hungarian kingdom to be rebuilt.
uncertaintyNote: Thomas of Split is a near-contemporary witness and supports the itinerary at regional scale. Exact days are uncertain. The pack deliberately makes no claim about why the Mongols withdrew. Carpini links it to Ögedei's death (11 December 1241). Modern historians also point to pasture and supply, losses, the succession politics Batu faced, or a raid that had already done its job. No single cause is proven. The shaded area is a regional footprint, not a route.
sources: Thomas of Split, Historia Salonitana chs. 36-39, especially withdrawal itinerary in ch.39 (Racki ed.; Sweeney source analysis 1981 pp.157-170)
Roger of Torre Maggiore, Carmen Miserabile
John of Plano Carpini, Ystoria Mongalorum
Jackson, The Mongols and the West
Sverdrup, The Mongol Conquests

title: Second Mongol invasion of Poland: Sandomierz and Kraków

sides.focus: Ulus of Jochi (Golden Horde) with Rus' auxiliaries

summary: In the winter of 1259–60 a Mongol-led army invaded Lesser Poland, took the town and castle of Sandomierz, and moved on towards Kraków before withdrawing.
detail: Eighteen years after the first invasion, Mongol armies came back into Poland from the east. Galicia–Volhynia had just been forced back under Horde control, and its princes had to supply troops. Długosz describes a winter invasion that crossed the Vistula lands, took Sandomierz town and then its castle, and moved on to Kraków, whose surroundings were plundered. The raiders then withdrew east with their booty and captives. Lesser Poland, which had barely recovered from 1241, was devastated a second time, and a third invasion followed in 1287–88.
significance: The invasion showed that the Horde could still strike deep into Central Europe. It confirmed Mongol control over the Rus' principalities along the Polish border.
uncertaintyNote: The pack follows Długosz, a fifteenth-century writer, for the course of events but leaves out his named commanders (Burundai, with Nogai and Talabuga), the duration, the massacre scenes (including the martyrdom of the Sandomierz Dominicans) and all totals, pending closer contemporary corroboration. Sandomierz is usually said to have fallen in February 1260. The pins mark Sandomierz and Kraków only; no route is implied.
sources: https://pl.wikisource.org/wiki/Strona:Jana_D%C5%82ugosza_Dziej%C3%B3w_Polskich_ksi%C4%85g_dwana%C5%9Bcie_-_Tom_II.djvu/372
https://pl.wikisource.org/wiki/Strona:Jana_D%C5%82ugosza_Dziej%C3%B3w_Polskich_ksi%C4%85g_dwana%C5%9Bcie_-_Tom_II.djvu/373
Jan Długosz, Annales seu Cronicae incliti Regni Poloniae

title: Mongol incursion into central Tibet: Reting and Gyal Lhakhang
place: Central Tibet, north of Lhasa (Reting and Gyal Lhakhang)

sides.opponent: Tibetan monastic communities and local lords

summary: In 1240 a Mongol force sent by Prince Köten entered central Tibet and burned the Kadampa monasteries of Reting and Gyal Lhakhang.
detail: Köten, a son of Ögedei, ruled the former Tangut lands on Tibet's north-eastern edge. In 1240 he sent a force south under Doorda Darqan. Tibetan historical works record the army's arrival and the burning of Reting (Rwa sgreng), the mother monastery of the Kadampa school, and of Gyal Lhakhang, with loss of life among the monks. The Mongols did not occupy the country. The expedition gathered intelligence on Tibet's religious and political leaders. It led to Köten's invitation to Sakya Pandita and the Mongol–Sakya relationship that followed.
significance: The incursion began direct Mongol involvement in Tibet and led to the lama–patron relationship that shaped Tibetan politics for a century.
uncertaintyNote: The pack names only the attacks on the two institutions and does not adopt the numbers of dead monks given in Tibetan histories, which are late and inconsistent. Wylie argued that the violence has been exaggerated and that this was more a reconnaissance than a conquest. The shaded area covers both monasteries without claiming exact points. The raid happened on the Tibetan frontier, not in Europe; it is tagged 'west' only because of the date span.
sources: https://library.bdrc.io/show/bdr:MW1KG5762
http://hdl.handle.net/2433/235463
Wylie, 'The First Mongol Conquest of Tibet Reinterpreted'
Petech, Central Tibet and the Mongols
Atwood, Encyclopedia of Mongolia and the Mongol Empire

title: Renewed Mongol campaign in central Tibet under Möngke
summary: Soon after Möngke's accession, a Mongol command advanced again into central Tibet in 1252–53. This built on the 1240 incursion and the Sakya submission, and moved towards direct military and administrative control.
detail: Möngke's reign brought a systematic reorganisation of the empire's conquered lands, and Tibet was part of it. The Yuanshi records renewed military activity in the Tibetan borderlands under his rule. Tibetan traditions remember a second Mongol army entering central Tibet in the early 1250s. Around the same time, Möngke divided Tibet's monastic houses among his brothers and kinsmen as patrons, and ordered a census and taxation. The Sakya lamas, already linked to Köten's house, soon passed under Kublai's patronage. Sakya Pandita's nephew Phagpa joined Kublai's court and later became his imperial preceptor.
significance: The campaign moved Mongol rule in Tibet from nominal submission towards the appanage and census system that the Yuan later organised under Sakya leadership.
uncertaintyNote: The pack accepts a renewed 1252–53 campaign but not a single commander. Tibetan sources variously name Qoridai or Doorda and may merge several expeditions. How far the army went and what it did are unclear. The shaded area shows only the general theatre; no route, battle site or control zone is implied.
sources: https://zh.wikisource.org/wiki/%E5%85%83%E5%8F%B2/%E5%8D%B7003
https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/journal-of-the-royal-asiatic-society/article/abs/mongol-conquest-of-tibet/B119D9D83ED5D11B6FA71790955F27DE
Petech, Central Tibet and the Mongols
Wylie, 'The First Mongol Conquest of Tibet Reinterpreted'

title: Conquest of the Kingdom of Dali and the Yunnan campaigns
summary: Kublai, ordered to take Dali in 1252, marched through the mountains of the Tibetan borderland in 1253 and took the capital. Uriyangkhadai then subdued the rest of Yunnan and captured King Duan Xingzhi in 1254.
detail: Möngke wanted to outflank the Song from the south-west. Kublai received the command in 1252 and set out the next year with Uriyangkhadai as his senior general. The Yuanshi describes the approach through the Jinsha River and its gorges, and the columns converging on Dali, which fell around the turn of 1253–54. The chief minister Gao Taixiang, blamed for killing Mongol envoys, was executed. Kublai's biographers stress that, on the advice of his Confucian counsellors, he forbade a general massacre. Kublai went north, and Uriyangkhadai continued campaigning in 1254. He took Shanchan (Kunming), captured Duan Xingzhi, and brought the peoples of Yunnan under Mongol rule. Duan was kept on as a Mongol-appointed ruler.
significance: The conquest brought Yunnan into the Mongol Empire, and so eventually into China, outflanked the Song, and made Kublai's name as a ruler willing to use restraint.
uncertaintyNote: The Yuanshi dates the fall of Dali to the 12th lunar month of 1253, which is late December 1253 or January 1254. The pack treats the conquest as a series of campaign phases with Dali and Shanchan as markers only. The march route and river crossings are not mapped. Army size is unknown; the traditional 100,000 is probably too high. The emphasis on Kublai's restraint comes from Confucian biographers.
sources: https://zh.wikisource.org/wiki/%E5%85%83%E5%8F%B2/%E5%8D%B7121
https://zh.wikisource.org/zh-hans/%E5%85%83%E5%8F%B2/%E5%8D%B7004
Rashid al-Din, Jami' al-Tawarikh

title: Jalairtai's invasions and Goryeo's negotiated submission
place: Goryeo (Korea), with the court on Ganghwa Island
casualties: The Goryeosa claims 206,800 people carried off in 1254 alone, with the dead beyond counting. The claim is plausible in scale but cannot be checked
summary: From 1254 Jalairtai's armies repeatedly ravaged Korea to force the island court to submit. After a 1258 coup overthrew the Choe military regime, Goryeo agreed terms, and in 1259 the crown prince travelled to the Mongols to do homage.
detail: Since 1232 Goryeo's court had sheltered on Ganghwa Island, across a strait the Mongol cavalry could not cross, while the mainland suffered invasion after invasion. From 1254 Jalairtai ran a campaign of deliberate devastation across the peninsula. The Goryeosa's figures for captives and dead are the worst of the whole war. The strain broke the military dictatorship. In 1258 officers including Kim Jun killed the last Choe dictator, Choe Ui, and the court turned to negotiation. In 1259 Crown Prince Wang Jeon set out to meet Möngke. He found the khan dead and met Kublai instead, who welcomed him. King Gojong died that year, and the prince became King Wonjong with Mongol backing.
significance: The negotiated submission ended nearly three decades of invasion and began Goryeo's long alliance, through royal marriages, with Kublai's dynasty.
uncertaintyNote: The pack treats 1254–59 as a phase of invasion and negotiation, not as the end of all resistance. The court did not return to the mainland until 1270, and the Sambyeolcho revolt lasted until 1273. The Korean and Chinese chronicles number and date the individual invasions differently. The shaded area is the whole peninsula; no routes or battle points are implied.
sources: https://ctext.org/wiki.pl?if=en&res=730924
https://ijkh.khistory.org/upload/pdf/10_03.pdf
Goryeosa
Yuanshi
Henthorn, Korea: The Mongol Invasions

title: First Mongol invasion of Đại Việt
place: Upper Red River delta: Bình Lệ Nguyên, Thăng Long and Đông Bộ Đầu
summary: Uriyangkhadai came down from Yunnan, defeated the Trần army at Bình Lệ Nguyên, and occupied the capital, Thăng Long. After about nine days, and a Vietnamese counter-attack at Đông Bộ Đầu, the Mongols withdrew.
detail: The Mongols had sent envoys asking for passage south to attack the Song, and Đại Việt had imprisoned them. In the winter of 1257–58 Uriyangkhadai led an army from Yunnan down into the delta. The Vietnamese annals describe King Trần Thái Tông leading his army, with war elephants, to Bình Lệ Nguyên, where it was beaten. The king withdrew by river. The Yuanshi records the defeat of Đại Việt's land and river forces and the Mongol entry into the capital, where they found their envoys still bound. The occupation lasted only about nine days. The Vietnamese annals record a counter-attack at Đông Bộ Đầu that drove the invaders out. Soon afterwards Đại Việt sent envoys, and a tributary relationship followed.
significance: This was the first of three Mongol invasions of Vietnam. It ended in nominal tribute rather than conquest.
uncertaintyNote: The Vietnamese annals date Bình Lệ Nguyên to the 12th day and Đông Bộ Đầu to the 24th day of the 12th lunar month of 1257. In the Western calendar these fall around 17 and 29 January 1258, so the event is shown from December 1257 to February 1258. The two traditions disagree on the ending: the Vietnamese record a victory, the Yuanshi a withdrawal followed by submission. The pack does not adopt the reports of a massacre in the capital, which have not been reconciled. The markers are named places only; no route is implied.
sources: https://zh.wikisource.org/zh-hant/%E5%A4%A7%E8%B6%8A%E5%8F%B2%E8%A8%98%E5%85%A8%E6%9B%B8/%E6%9C%AC%E7%B4%80%E5%8D%B7%E4%B9%8B%E4%BA%94
https://zh.wikisource.org/wiki/%E5%85%83%E5%8F%B2/%E5%8D%B7209
Atwood, Encyclopedia of Mongolia and the Mongol Empire

title: Siege and capture of Erzurum (Theodosiopolis/Karin)
summary: Baiju, the new Mongol commander in the Caucasus, besieged and took the Seljuk frontier city of Erzurum. This opened the Mongol invasion of Anatolia.
detail: With Georgia and Armenia subdued, the Mongol army based on the Mughan steppe turned west against the Seljuk Sultanate of Rum. Baiju had replaced Chormaqan as commander. Erzurum, the old Byzantine Theodosiopolis and Armenian Karin, guarded the high road from the Araxes into Anatolia. Kirakos Gandzaketsi, a contemporary Armenian historian, describes the Mongols surrounding the city, setting up siege engines, and breaking in after a hard fight. Many of the inhabitants, Christian and Muslim, were killed or carried off. The fall of the frontier fortress exposed the Seljuk heartland, and the decisive battle followed the next summer.
significance: Erzurum's fall opened Anatolia to the Mongols and led directly to Köse Dağ.
uncertaintyNote: Kirakos places the siege in 1242, and it may have ended early in 1243. The pack leaves out the massacre rhetoric in the sources. The siege lasted about two months. This belongs to the Anatolian story of Baiju rather than the European campaign; it is tagged 'west' because it began in 1242.
sources: Kirakos Gandzakets’i, History of the Armenians ch.34 (Bedrosian trans.)
Bar Hebraeus, Chronography
Jackson, The Mongols and the Islamic World
Dashdondog, The Mongols and the Armenians (1220–1335)

title: Battle of Köse Dağ
summary: Baiju's army defeated the Seljuk sultan Kaykhusraw II at Köse Dağ. The sultan fled, and Seljuk Rum became a Mongol tributary.
detail: Kaykhusraw II gathered a large, mixed army against the invaders, with Turkish troops, Latin mercenaries and contingents from his Christian neighbours. The armies met in the mountains near Köse Dağ, west of Erzincan. Kirakos calls the place Ch'man-katuk. The Mongol vanguard broke the sultan's army, and Kaykhusraw fled west, abandoning his camp. Sivas submitted. Kayseri resisted and was sacked. The sultan's ministers negotiated tribute, and neighbouring rulers hurried to make their own terms. Hethum I of Cilician Armenia, for instance, handed over the sultan's fleeing family to the Mongols.
significance: Köse Dağ ended the power of the Seljuk Sultanate of Rum, which became a Mongol vassal. It opened the political fragmentation of Anatolia from which the Ottomans would later emerge.
uncertaintyNote: 26 June 1243 is the usual date; some sources give 3 July. The pack leaves out army totals: the chronicles' Seljuk figures (60,000–80,000) are inflated. It also leaves out an exact battle point, so the shaded area covers the region the sources describe. Whether the Seljuks broke almost without fighting, as some accounts suggest, is debated.
sources: Kirakos Gandzakets’i, History of the Armenians ch.35 (Bedrosian trans.)
Ibn Bibi, al-Awamir al-'Ala'iyya
Bar Hebraeus, Chronography
Jackson, The Mongols and the Islamic World
May, The Mongol Conquests in World History

title: Surrender of Maymun-Diz and Alamut
summary: Hülegü's armies surrounded the Nizari Ismaili Imam, Rukn al-Din Khurshah, at Maymun-Diz. He surrendered on 19 November 1256, and Alamut, the famous 'Eagle's Nest', gave up in early December.
detail: Möngke had given his brother Hülegü two tasks in the west: destroy the Nizari Ismailis, the 'Assassins' of Western legend, and bring the Abbasid caliph to heel. After months of negotiation, in which Khurshah gave up minor castles while keeping his strongholds, three Mongol columns closed on the Alamut valley. Juvaini, who was present, describes the bombardment of Maymun-Diz with engines and a long-range crossbow, and the Imam coming down with his family on 19 November. At his order most castles surrendered. Alamut's garrison held out briefly and then yielded. Juvaini went through its famous library, saved some books and instruments, and burned what he judged heretical. The fortress was then dismantled.
significance: These surrenders destroyed the Nizari state that had resisted the Seljuks and the caliphate for more than a century and a half. The road to Baghdad was now clear.
uncertaintyNote: The dates come from Juvaini, a participant: 19 November for Maymun-Diz and early December for Alamut (some reckon mid-December). The pack deliberately does not claim that Nizari territory was wholly extinguished. Girdkuh held out until 1270 and Lambsar for over a year, and Juvaini, himself hostile, gives only general reports of later massacres. Maymun-Diz has not been securely located; the marker uses Majidi's Mount Shatan identification, and Shams Kalayeh is an alternative.
sources: Juvayni, History of the World-Conqueror vol. II, ch. VII, pp.618-638 (Boyle trans.)
Rashid al-Din, Jami' al-Tawarikh
Daftary, The Isma'ilis: Their History and Doctrines
Willey, Eagle's Nest: Ismaili Castles in Iran and Syria
Jackson, The Mongols and the Islamic World

title: Battle between Konya and Aksaray
place: Between Konya and Aksaray, central Anatolia
summary: Pushed west into Anatolia by Hülegü's arrival in Iran, Baiju demanded winter quarters from Sultan Kaykaus II. When he refused, Baiju defeated him and installed his brother Rukn al-Din (Kılıç Arslan IV).
detail: After Kaykhusraw II's death the Seljuk throne was contested between his sons, and the Mongols played them against each other. When Hülegü arrived in Iran, Baiju's army had to leave the Mughan pastures and move into Anatolia. Bar Hebraeus says Baiju asked for winter quarters. Kaykaus II refused and met him in battle beside a caravanserai, a khan, between Konya and Aksaray. The sultan's army was beaten, and Kaykaus fled to the Byzantines. Baiju placed his brother Rukn al-Din on the throne. The sultanate was now divided between puppet rulers whose ministers answered to the Mongols. Baiju soon went on to join Hülegü's march on Baghdad.
significance: The battle turned the Seljuk Sultanate into a Mongol protectorate in all but name, divided between rival sultans.
uncertaintyNote: Other sources give 14 or 15 October 1256. The battle is often placed at the Sultan Hanı caravanserai near Aksaray, but the pack follows Bar Hebraeus's broader 'between Konya and Aksaray', and the shaded area reflects that. Ibn Bibi's fuller account is partisan.
sources: https://archive.org/stream/BarHebraeusChronography/BarHebraeus_Chronography_djvu.txt
https://archive.org/details/BarHebraeusChronography
Ibn Bibi, al-Awamir al-'Ala'iyya
Jackson, The Mongols and the Islamic World

title: Siege and capture of Baghdad; end of the Abbasid Caliphate
summary: Hülegü's armies surrounded Baghdad on both banks of the Tigris and battered their way onto its walls, and Caliph al-Musta'sim surrendered. The city was sacked and the caliph put to death, ending five centuries of Abbasid rule there.
detail: Al-Musta'sim rejected Hülegü's summons, trusting that the Islamic world would rise in his defence. In January 1258 Mongol columns closed in from the east, while Baiju's army came across the Tigris from the west, destroyed the caliph's field army and cut off escape downriver. Siege engines built by Chinese engineers pounded the eastern walls until the Mongols held the ramparts. The caliph came out with his sons and officials and surrendered. The city was then plundered. Kirakos Gandzaketsi drew his account from an eyewitness, the Armenian prince Prosh, who served in the Mongol army. He describes Christians being spared in their churches while palaces and mosques burned. On 20 February the caliph was killed.
significance: The fall of Baghdad ended the Abbasid Caliphate in Iraq, shocked the Islamic world, and made Hülegü's Ilkhanate the dominant power of the Middle East.
uncertaintyNote: The main dates are fairly secure: investment in late January, surrender on 10 February, the caliph's death on 20 February. The pack gives no death toll and no length for the sack, and leaves out the atrocity rhetoric. Chronicle totals run from 800,000 (Rashid al-Din) to 2 million, and modern historians give no reliable figure. How the caliph died is told in several ways: rolled in a carpet and trampled, starved among his treasure (Marco Polo), or simply killed. Blaming the Shi'i vizier Ibn al-'Alqami for betrayal is a Sunni polemic.
sources: Kirakos Gandzakets’i, History of the Armenians ch.60 (Bedrosian trans.; eyewitness account attributed to Prince Prosh)
Rashid al-Din, Jami' al-Tawarikh
Nasir al-Din Tusi, account of the fall of Baghdad (appended to Juvaini)
Jackson, The Mongols and the Islamic World
Morgan, The Mongols

title: The Mongols fortify Lizhou as a base in Sichuan
summary: Instead of raiding Sichuan and pulling out, Möngke's government ordered Lizhou fortified in 1252 as a permanent forward base. Garrison farms followed in 1253, and fighting continued around Lizhou in 1254.
detail: Mongol armies had been raiding Sichuan since 1236 and then withdrawing, and the Song kept recovering the ground. Soon after his accession, Möngke changed the approach. The Yuanshi records an order in 1252 to fortify Lizhou, the gateway town on the Jialing River below the Jianmen pass. The Wang family of Gongchang, Mongol-allied generals, led by Wang Dechen, carried it out, repairing the walls and setting soldiers to farm the land to feed the garrison. The Songshi records the Mongol fortification of Lizhou and Langzhou and fighting around Lizhou in 1254. From this base Möngke's own invasion of Sichuan was launched in 1258.
significance: Lizhou gave the Mongols a permanent base inside Sichuan, preparing the great offensive of 1258–59.
uncertaintyNote: The Yuanshi and Songshi independently confirm the fortification. The pack marks Lizhou, with Langzhou as a secondary marker, and draws no garrison zone or supply route. Wang Dechen's leading role comes from his Yuanshi biography.
sources: https://zh.wikisource.org/wiki/%E5%85%83%E5%8F%B2/%E5%8D%B7003
https://zh.wikisource.org/wiki/%E5%AE%8B%E5%8F%B2/%E5%8D%B7044
Allsen, 'The Rise of the Mongolian Empire and Mongolian Rule in North China', Cambridge History of China vol. 6
Atwood, Encyclopedia of Mongolia and the Mongol Empire

title: Möngke decides on war with the Song
place: Möngke's court in Mongolia (seasonal camp not located)
summary: In summer 1256 Möngke's princes asked for war on the Southern Song, and he agreed, citing the Song's detention of Mongol envoys. In 1257 he ordered the princes to march and decided to lead the campaign himself.
detail: Möngke had spent the first years of his reign securing his throne and sending his brothers to Yunnan and Iran. The Yuanshi records a council in the summer of 1256 at which the princes asked to attack the Song. Möngke agreed, giving the Song's detention of Mongol envoys as the reason. In 1257 the order to mobilise followed. Möngke chose to lead the army himself, the first Great Khan to take the field in person since Chinggis. The plan was a three-pronged attack. Möngke would invade Sichuan from the north, Kublai would strike at the middle Yangtze, and Uriyangkhadai would come up from Yunnan through the south.
significance: The decision committed the whole empire to the conquest of the Song. It led to Möngke's death at Diaoyu and the succession war that followed.
uncertaintyNote: The pack treats this as a court-level political and mobilisation phase with no map geometry. The shaded area only marks Möngke's court region in Mongolia; the actual camp is not located, and the halo does not mean the council took place at Karakorum. The Yuanshi months are lunar: the pack's 'June 1256' corresponds roughly to July 1256 in the Western calendar. Around the same time Möngke had Kublai's administration audited, and some historians see a rift between the brothers behind Möngke's choice to command in person.
sources: https://zh.wikisource.org/wiki/%E5%85%83%E5%8F%B2/%E5%8D%B7003
https://zh.wikisource.org/wiki/%E5%AE%8B%E5%8F%B2/%E5%8D%B7044
Rossabi, Khubilai Khan: His Life and Times
Allsen, Mongol Imperialism

title: Song counter-attack on Chengdu defeated
summary: In 1258 the Song commander in Sichuan, Pu Zezhi, attacked Mongol-held Chengdu and was defeated by Niulin. Mongol guards stayed in the city while Möngke's campaign moved south.
detail: Chengdu had been sacked in 1236 and had changed hands in the years of raiding that followed. As Möngke's great invasion of Sichuan got under way, the Mongol general Niulin held the Chengdu plain. The Song commander Pu Zezhi tried to recover the city. The Yuanshi records his defeat by Niulin and the Mongol decision to leave a garrison in Chengdu as the main army moved south-east towards Chongqing and the Diaoyu fortress. The Songshi confirms from the Song side that Chengdu was not recovered despite long campaigning. Holding it secured the rear of Möngke's advance.
significance: The failed counter-attack left the Chengdu plain in Mongol hands, securing Möngke's rear as he advanced on Diaoyu.
uncertaintyNote: Both Chinese chronicles confirm the event, but they give no forces, casualties or exact date within 1258. The pack treats it as a city-level counter-offensive, not a full siege.
sources: https://zh.wikisource.org/wiki/%E5%85%83%E5%8F%B2/%E5%8D%B7003
https://zh.wikisource.org/wiki/%E5%AE%8B%E5%8F%B2/%E5%8D%B7044
Allsen, 'The Rise of the Mongolian Empire and Mongolian Rule in North China', Cambridge History of China vol. 6
Atwood, Encyclopedia of Mongolia and the Mongol Empire

title: Siege of Diaoyu Fortress and the death of Möngke Khan
summary: Möngke's army attacked the Song stronghold on Diaoyu Mountain again and again for about five months but could not take it. The khan fell ill and died there in August 1259, and the united empire's last great offensive collapsed.
detail: Diaoyu stood on a steep hill where the Jialing, Fu and Qu rivers meet. It was fortified to stand a long siege, with fields and springs inside its walls. Möngke had overrun much of northern Sichuan, and from early 1259 he threw his army against it. Yuanshi biographies record assaults driven back and the death of the vanguard general Wang Dechen beneath the walls. The Song commander Wang Jian held out. The Yuanshi says Möngke fell ill in the summer and died at Diaoyu Mountain. His body was taken back to Mongolia. News of his death halted Hülegü's advance in the west and prompted Kublai and Ariq Böke to prepare their claims to the throne.
significance: Diaoyu was one of the few places where the Mongols clearly failed. Möngke's death there started the Toluid civil war and the break-up of the united empire.
uncertaintyNote: The Yuanshi records the illness in the 6th lunar month and the death in the 7th. The pack writes these as 'June' and 'July', but in the Western calendar the death falls on 11 August 1259, the date used here. The pack gives no cause of death: Rashid al-Din and the Yuanshi point to disease (dysentery or cholera), while later Chinese tradition says he was wounded by a missile. Stories of the defenders throwing fresh fish over the walls come from later local tradition. The shaded area covers the fortress hill.
sources: Yuan shi 元史, juan 3, Xianzong benji 憲宗本紀, Xianzong 9 (Chinese original; my translation for atlas wording)
Yuan shi 元史, juan 155, Wang Shixian zhuan 汪世顯傳, Wang Dechen section; juan 155 Shi Tianze zhuan 史天澤傳 (Chinese originals; my translation)
Rashid al-Din, Jami' al-Tawarikh
Rossabi, Khubilai Khan: His Life and Times
Allsen, Mongol Imperialism

title: Kublai crosses the Yangtze, besieges Ezhou, and withdraws
place: Ezhou (modern Wuchang, Wuhan), on the Yangtze
summary: Kublai crossed the Yangtze and surrounded Ezhou in autumn 1259, even after hearing of Möngke's death. Late in the year, with reports that Ariq Böke was mobilising in the north, he broke off and returned north.
detail: Kublai led the eastern wing of the 1259 offensive. He crossed the Huai, reached the Yangtze, and learned that his brother had died. The Yuanshi says he refused to turn back without achieving something. His army crossed the great river under fire and surrounded Ezhou on the south bank. The Song sent the minister Jia Sidao to relieve it. Kublai's wife Chabi sent word that Ariq Böke was raising troops, and Kublai disengaged in stages and marched north late in the year. Song writers later said Jia had bought him off with a secret peace, promising tribute and the Yangtze as a border. Jia reported a great victory.
significance: The crossing showed that the Yangtze could be forced. Kublai's withdrawal led straight into his war with Ariq Böke for the throne.
uncertaintyNote: The Yuanshi months are lunar. The 9th month, when the pack says 'September', runs from about late September into October 1259, so the crossing and investment are shown at month precision. The pack does not treat the secret peace as the sole reason for the withdrawal: the Yuanshi stresses the succession crisis, while the secret-peace story comes from later Song historiography hostile to Jia Sidao.
sources: Yuan shi 元史, juan 4, Shizu benji 世祖本紀, pre-accession Jiwei year (Chinese original; my translation for atlas wording)
Song shi jishi benmo 宋史紀事本末, juan 102, Menggu qin Song 蒙古侵宋, Kaiqing 1 (Chinese original; my translation)
Rossabi, Khubilai Khan: His Life and Times
